hints: Recall what the term zwitterion means for the $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COOH}$ groups at the isoelectric point.
walkthrough:
Picture what isoelectric point means**
At pH 6.0 valine has no net charge. Think of the neutral amino acid $H_{2}N-CH(R)-COOH$ transferring a proton internally from the carboxylic acid to the amine. You end up with both charges in the same molecule.

Build valine as its zwitterion**
Valine has R = $CH(CH_{3})_{2}$. Keep the central $CH$ joined to R, to $^{+}NH_{3}$ and to $COO^{-}$. So write $^{+}H_{3}N-CH(CH(CH_{3})_{2})-C(=O)-O^{-}$. The $NH_{3}^{+}$ gives +1 and the $COO^{-}$ gives -1, net charge zero.

hints: Write out lysine with its three ionisable groups: alpha-$\text{COOH}$, alpha-$\text{NH}_{2}$ and side chain $(CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2}$.
Think about what adding $H^{+}$ from sulfuric acid does to $COO^{-}$ to give $COOH$ and to $NH_{2}$ to give $NH_{3}^{+}$.
At very low pH 1.0 all basic sites are protonated, so count the charges to predict the fully protonated +2 ion.
walkthrough:
Start from lysine at pH 9.7**
Lysine is $H_{2}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2})-COOH$ in neutral form. At its isoelectric point pH 9.7 it is a neutral zwitterion, mainly $H_{2}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{3}^{+})-COO^{-}$. Net charge = 0 from $-1 + 1$. Adding acid will protonate $COO^{-}$ and $NH_{2}$ groups step by step.

Form the +1 ions for boxes A and B**
Adding one $H^{+}$ gives net +1. There are three isomeric ways to write a +1 ion, all with two protons added to the fully deprotonated backbone relative to high pH:
$^{+}H_{3}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{3}^{+})-COO^{-}$ (both nitrogens protonated, carboxylate still deprotonated)
$^{+}H_{3}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2})-COOH$ (alpha nitrogen protonated, carboxylic acid protonated)
$H_{2}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{3}^{+})-COOH$ (side chain nitrogen protonated, carboxylic acid protonated)
Pick any two different ones for A and B. Check charge: e.g. $+1 +1 -1 = +1$.

Push to pH 1.0 for box C**
At pH 1.0, well below all $pK_{a}$ values, every group that can take a proton has taken one. $COO^{-}$ becomes $COOH$, alpha $NH_{2}$ becomes $^{+}NH_{3}$, side chain $NH_{2}$ becomes $^{+}NH_{3}$. That gives $^{+}H_{3}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{3}^{+})-C(=O)-OH$ with charge $+1 +1 +0 = +2$.

Final answer: Box A and Box B (any two different +1 ions, in any order):
A: $^{+}H_{3}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{3}^{+})-COO^{-}$
B: $^{+}H_{3}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2})-COOH$
(or $H_{2}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{3}^{+})-COOH$, also +1)
Box C (pH 1.0, +2 ion): $^{+}H_{3}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{3}^{+})-COOH$

hints: Remember Val-Lys means valine provides the $\text{-COOH}$ end and lysine provides the $\text{-NH}_{2}$ end for the new amide link.
Focus on drawing $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ with all atoms and bonds shown, keeping the two side chains unchanged.
walkthrough:
Line up the partners in the right order**
Val-Lys is read left to right from N terminus to C terminus. So put valine on the left as $H_{2}N-CH(CH(CH_{3})_{2})-COOH$ and lysine on the right as $H_{2}N-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2})-COOH$. The $COOH$ of Val joins to the $NH_{2}$ of Lys with loss of $H_{2}O$.

Draw the displayed peptide link**
Join them as $...-C(=O)-NH-...$. You must show the carbonyl double bond $C=O$ and the $N-H$ bond explicitly, not as $CONH$. The full dipeptide is $H_{2}N-CH(CH(CH_{3})_{2})-C(=O)-NH-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2})-C(=O)-OH$. Check: free $NH_{2}$ on Val end, free $COOH$ on Lys end, side chains $CH(CH_{3})_{2}$ and $(CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2}$ untouched.
Final answer: $H_{2}N-CH(CH(CH_{3})_{2})-C(=O)-NH-CH((CH_{2})_{4}NH_{2})-C(=O)-OH$ with $C=O$ and $N-H$ fully displayed in the peptide link.
